questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Khadar and Bhangar plains: 1. Bhangar consists of younger alluvium deposited by annual floods, forming fertile land without kankar. 2. Khadar consists of older, elevated alluvial terraces away from rivers, rich in kankar deposits. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect: • Khadar:

Khadar is younger alluvium found in lowlying floodplains along river channels. It consists mainly of fine silt and clay and is renewed every year by flood deposits. Kankar nodules are absent, and the soil is highly fertile.

Statement 2 is incorrect: • Bhangar:

Bhangar is located on elevated terraces above the floodplains. It contains old alluvium with kankar nodules and is less fertile than Khadar. Additional Facts: • Correct sequence from the Himalayan foothills towards the plains:

Bhabar → Terai → Bhangar → Khadar • Bihar-specific types of Bhangar:

Balsundari Soil: ◊ Found in North Bihar — Saran, Champaran, Muzaffarpur, and Saharsa. It is a loamy old alluvial soil containing lime nodules.

Karail–Kewal Soil: ◊ Found in South Bihar — Rohtas, Gaya, Patna, and Munger. It is a heavy, dark, clayey soil with high water-retention capacity. • Bihar-specific features of Khadar:

Khadar soils dominate the plains of North Bihar due to active river systems such as the Kosi, Gandak, and Bagmati.

Local term — Diara Land: ◊ Diara lands are fertile floodplain tracts and riverine islands that are flooded annually. ◊ These areas are particularly suitable for crops such as maize and watermelon. • Bhabar Zone — Piedmont Belt

The Bhabhar is a narrow belt located just south of the Shiwalik foothills.

It is about 8–10 km wide and consists mainly of coarse gravel and pebbles.

Due to its high porosity, rivers disappear underground in this zone, making it unsuitable for agriculture. • Terai Zone — Marshy Belt

The Terai lies immediately south of the Bhabar zone.

In this region, underground streams re-emerge, creating marshy and waterlogged conditions.

The area supports dense forests and fertile soils. • Bihar Terai belt:

Occurs as a narrow strip (3–8 km wide) along the northern districts of West Champaran, Sitamarhi, Araria, and Kishanganj.

These soils are suitable for crops such as sugarcane and jute.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Desert: 1. The underlying geological structure of the desert is a subsurface extension of the Peninsular Plateau. 2. questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: • The Indian Desert (Thar Desert) is a northwestern extension of the Peninsular Plateau. • Geological nature: Ancient peninsular rock base buried under aeolian (wind-blown) sand deposits. • Rock structure below the desert: Similar to Aravalli and Peninsular Plateau rocks. Supporting geological evidence:

Akal Wood Fossil Park (Jaisalmer): Contains fossilised tree trunks about 180 million years old.

Marine deposits near Brahmsar: Indicate that the region was once submerged under sea during the Mesozoic Era. Statement 2 is correct:

Luni River is the only major river system of the Indian Desert.

River type: Ephemeral (seasonal) river dependent on monsoon rainfall.

Origin: Pushkar Valley, Aravalli Range (Rajasthan).

Formation: Initially formed by streams such as the Saraswati and Sabarmati. Course characteristics:

Water remains fresh up to Balotra (Rajasthan).

Beyond Balotra: Water becomes saline due to desert salts.

Drainage type: Inland drainage (endorheic).

End point: Drains into Rann of Kutch (Gujarat). Additional Facts:

Indian Desert (Thar Desert) Features:

Location: Western Rajasthan and adjoining Gujarat region.

Climate type: Arid to semi-arid.

Major wind action: Formation of aeolian sand dunes. Dominant dune type:

Barchans — crescent-shaped sand dunes common near Jaisalmer. Local geographic terms:

Marusthali: Core desert region with shifting sand dunes.

Bagar (Bangar): Semi-arid transitional zone between Aravalli Range and desert. Desert Drainage and Lakes

Drainage type: Inland drainage dominant.

Seasonal streams: Flow only during monsoon months.

Important saline lakes (Playas): • Sambhar Lake: Largest inland salt lake in India. • Didwana Lake • Pachpadra Lake

Definition: • Playa: Temporary saline lake formed in desert depressions. Luni River:

Origin: Aravalli Range near Pushkar

Nature: Seasonal desert river

Water quality change point: Balotra Final drainage: Rann of Kutch

Meaning of name: “Luni” means salt river Statement 3 is incorrect:

The Indian Desert (Thar Desert) receives very low rainfall, generally below 150 mm annually in its core region.

This extremely low rainfall creates highly arid conditions with sparse vegetation.

The driest central part of the desert is called Marusthali, meaning the most arid and barren zone of the Thar Desert. Statement 4 is correct:

The surface of the Indian Desert shows undulating topography mainly shaped by wind (aeolian) action.

The region is dotted with characteristic sand dune forms such as: • Barchans — crescent-shaped dunes formed due to unidirectional winds. • Longitudinal dunes (Seifs) — long sand ridges aligned parallel to prevailing wind direction.

These dune types are widespread across western Rajasthan, especially around Jaisalmer and Barmer regions. Additional Facts:

Desert Zones of Rajasthan

Moving westward from the Aravalli Range, the desert shows clear transitional zones:

Aravalli Range: • Acts as a climatic barrier, limiting the reach of monsoon rainfall toward western Rajasthan.

Rajasthan Bagar: • Semi-arid transitional zone west of the Aravallis. • Contains sparse scrub vegetation and seasonal streams.

Marusthali: • Core arid region of the Thar Desert. • Dominated by sand dunes and barren terrain.

questions.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The distance between two longitudes decreases as we move towards the poles. 2. The distance between two latitudes varies from the equator to the poles. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: • The distance between two longitudes decreases as we move towards the poles. • Reason: Longitudes are semicircles that converge at the North and South Poles. • Maximum distance between longitudes occurs at the Equator. • Distance between 1° longitude at Equator: About 111.3 km. • Distance between longitudes gradually decreases towards higher latitudes. • At the Poles, the distance between longitudes becomes zero because all longitudes meet.

Statement 2 is incorrect: • Latitudes are parallel circles that never meet. • Distance between two latitudes is generally constant. • Distance between 1° latitude: About 111 km everywhere on Earth (standard textbook value).

Important note: • Though Earth is slightly flattened at poles (oblate spheroid), this variation is very small and usually ignored in standard geography questions.

Additional Facts: • Latitudes — Core Properties

Latitudes are parallel circles running east–west.

They never intersect each other.

Distance between successive latitudes: About 111 km.

Total number of latitudes: 180 (90° North + 90° South).

Special latitude: • Equator (0° latitude) is the largest latitude. • It divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

Longitudes — Core Properties • Longitudes are semicircles running north–south. • They converge at the poles. • Total number of longitudes: 360. • Distance pattern:

Maximum at Equator.

Decreases steadily toward poles.

Zero distance at poles.

Great Circles — Key Facts • Equator is the only latitude that forms a Great Circle. • Any pair of opposite longitudes forms a Great Circle. • Great Circles represent the shortest distance between two points on Earth.

Pir Panjal is the longest range of the Lesser Himalayas (Himachal Himalaya).

The Lesser Himalayas consist of several important ranges, among which Pir Panjal is the longest and most significant.

Geographically, it extends from the Jhelum River in the northwest to the upper Beas River region in Himachal Pradesh.

It also forms a major natural barrier separating the Kashmir Valley from the plains to the south. Dhaula Dhar:

Dhaula Dhar is a prominent range of the Lesser Himalayas, mainly located in Himachal Pradesh.

However, it is shorter than the Pir Panjal range. Shiwalik:

The Shiwalik Range belongs to the Outer Himalayas, not the Lesser Himalayas.

It is the southernmost Himalayan range, composed mainly of loose sediments.

Therefore, it cannot be the longest range of the Lesser Himalayas. Zanskar:

The Zanskar Range lies north of the Great Himalayas.

It belongs to the Trans-Himalayan region, not the Lesser Himalayas.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the structural evolution of the Himalayas: 1. The Greater Himalayas and the Lesser Himalayas are separated by the Main Central Thrust. 2. Statement 2 is correct: The Lesser Himalayas and Shiwaliks are separated by the Main Boundary Thrust (MBT). This boundary developed during later stages of mountain building. • The Himalayas evolved through multiple phases of uplift. Around 45 million years ago, a major uplift created rugged ranges like Pir Panjal Dhauladhar and Mahabharat. • Intermontane basins such as Kashmir valley and Kathmandu valleys were formed between these ranges. • The Shiwaliks were formed by thick terrestrial sediments during the Miocene to Pleistocene period. • These deposits reflect continuous uplift and erosion of the Himalayas. • The Himalayan Front Fault (HFF) marks the boundary with the Northern Plains and remains tectonically active.

questions.q: Assertion (A): India has selected 82°30’ E longitude as its standard meridian. Reason (R): Standard meridians are chosen at multiples of 7°30’ longitude, as each such multiple corresponds to exactly 30 minutes of time difference from UTC. Select the correct answer:

questions.explanation:
Assertion (A) is true: • India has selected 82°30’ E longitude as its Standard Meridian. • This longitude determines Indian Standard Time (IST) for the entire country. • The standard meridian passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, which is centrally located in India.

Reason (R) is true: • Standard meridians across the world are chosen at multiples of 7°30’ (7.5°). • This rule is based on the Earth’s rotation:

Key relation: • Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours • Therefore, 15° longitude = 1 hour

3 7°30’ longitude = 30 minutes Thus, choosing meridians at multiples of 7°30’ allows time to be expressed neatly in whole hours or half-hours from UTC. Why (R) correctly explains (A):

India selected 82°30’ E (82.5° E) because: • It is a multiple of 7°30’, satisfying the global standard time system. • It gives a time difference of 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (UTC +5:30). Calculation:

5° ÷ 15° = 5.5 hours

Therefore, IST = UTC +5:30 Hence, the reason directly explains why 82°30’ E was chosen.

questions.q: Assertion (A): India’s longitudinal span causes about a 2-hour difference in sunrise between Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat. Reason (R): The Earth rotates from west to east, making eastern locations experience sunrise earlier than western ones.

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.explanation:
Assertion (A) is correct:

India extends longitudinally from about 68°7′ E (Gujarat) to 97°25′ E (Arunachal Pradesh).

This gives a longitudinal extent of roughly 30 degrees.

Since the Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour, a 30-degree difference produces about a 2-hour difference in local sunrise between the easternmost and westernmost parts of India.

Therefore, sunrise occurs nearly 2 hours earlier in Arunachal Pradesh than in Gujarat. Reason (R) is correct:

The Earth rotates from west to east, which causes the Sun to appear to rise first in eastern locations and later in western locations.

This explains why eastern places see the sunrise earlier than western places. Why (R) is not the correct explanation of (A):

The Assertion talks about the magnitude of the time difference (about 2 hours).

The Reason explains only the direction of Earth’s rotation, not the amount of time difference.

To fully explain the 2-hour difference, the reason would need to include the rate of Earth’s rotation (15° per hour) and India’s 30° longitudinal extent.

Hence, both statements are true, but the reason does not fully explain the assertion. Additional Facts: Longitude–Time Relationship Key rules:

Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours

Therefore:

3 15° longitude = 1 hour

3 1° longitude = 4 minutes Application to India:

India’s longitude span ≈ 30°

Time difference:

3 30 × 4 minutes = 120 minutes (2 hours) Standard Time vs Local Time Local time:

Based on the Sun’s actual position at a location.

Would create different times across India. Standard time (IST):

Based on 82°30′ E longitude.

Used to maintain uniform time across the country.

questions.q: Which of the following regions is the origin of the cold and chilly winds that are obstructed by the Himalayan Mountains?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Siberian and Central Asian high-pressure region
options.C: Tibetan Plateau and adjoining Trans-Himalayan region

questions.explanation:
Cold winter winds affecting Asia originate from a strong high-pressure system formed over Siberia and Central Asia.

During winter, the Eurasian landmass cools intensely, creating a very high-pressure zone called the Siberian High.

Winds naturally flow from high pressure to low pressure, so cold, dry winds move outward from this region.

The Himalayan Mountains act as a massive physical barrier, preventing these extremely cold winds from entering the Indian subcontinent.

Because of this obstruction, India experiences comparatively milder winters than regions of Central Asia at similar latitudes.

Thus, the Siberian and Central Asian highpressure region is the correct origin of these cold winds. Additional Facts:

Role of the Siberian High in Winter Climate: • The Siberian High forms over Siberia and Central Asia during winter due to intense land cooling. • It is one of the strongest seasonal highpressure systems in the world. • It generates cold, dry continental winds that move outward toward surrounding regions. Role of the Himalayas as a Climatic Barrier:

The Himalayas perform two major climatic functions: • Blocking Cold Winds in Winter

Prevent freezing continental winds from Central Asia from reaching India. Without this barrier, North India would experience extremely harsh winters similar to Central Asia. • Intercepting Monsoon Winds in Summer

Force moist southwest monsoon winds to rise and produce rainfall.

Without the Himalayas, monsoon rainfall in northern India would be drastically reduced. Arctic Ocean marginal belt:

Extremely cold region, but not the direct source of winter winds affecting India. Tibetan Plateau and adjoining TransHimalayan region

Influences regional pressure patterns, but the primary cold wind origin remains SiberiaCentral Asia. Iranian Plateau and Caspian lowlands:

Associated with western disturbances, not the cold continental winds blocked by the Himalayas.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the role of Jet Streams in relation to winter cyclonic depressions in India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: They block the west-to-east movement of cyclonic depressions before reaching the Indian subcontinent
options.B: They significantly intensify the summer monsoon rainfall over the Indian region
options.C: They steer and guide the cyclonic depressions towards the northwestern parts of India
options.D: They transform shallow cyclonic depressions into intense tropical cyclones over land

questions.explanation:
Jet streams play a steering role in bringing winter cyclonic depressions (Western Disturbances) to India.

Western Disturbances originate as temperate cyclones over the Mediterranean region.

These disturbances are carried eastward by the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream.

During winter, this jet stream flows south of the Himalayas, acting like an atmospheric pathway.

As a result, these cyclonic systems are steered toward northwestern India, especially Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, and western Uttar Pradesh.

They bring winter rainfall and snowfall, which is crucial for agriculture and water resources.

Thus, the correct statement is that jet streams steer and guide cyclonic depressions toward northwestern India. Additional Facts:

Nature of Western Disturbances • Western Disturbances are extratropical (temperate) cyclones, not tropical cyclones. • They develop due to the interaction of cold polar air and warm subtropical air. • Their origin region is mainly the Mediterranean Sea. • They move from west to east, guided by upper-air westerlies. Role of the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream:

In winter, the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream shifts southward over northern India.

It carries Western Disturbances across West Asia, Pakistan, and into India.

When these disturbances encounter the Himalayas, they produce: • Rainfall in the northwestern plains • Snowfall in the Himalayan regions Agricultural Importance of Winter Rainfall:

Winter rainfall supports Rabi crops, especially: • Wheat • Mustard • Gram

In northwestern India, this rainfall is locally known as Mahawat.

Snowfall in the Himalayas helps recharge glaciers and rivers during summer.

questions.q: Which of the following regions in northeastern India receives the highest rainfall due to orographic effects?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Meghalaya Plateau receives the highest rainfall in northeastern India due to strong orographic (relief) rainfall.

The Bay of Bengal branch of the Southwest Monsoon carries large amounts of moisture toward northeastern India.

When these winds reach the Meghalaya Plateau, they encounter the steep slopes of the Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia Hills.

The hills are arranged in a funnel-like formation facing the Bay of Bengal.

This forces the moisture-laden air to rise rapidly, causing cooling, condensation, and extremely heavy rainfall on the windward slopes.

As a result, places such as Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Sohra) receive some of the highest rainfall totals in the world. Role of Orographic Rainfall in Meghalaya:

Moist winds from the Bay of Bengal strike the plateau directly.

The steep southern escarpment of the Khasi Hills forces sudden uplift of air.

This produces intense and prolonged rainfall during the monsoon season.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes a river basin from a watershed?

options.A: Watersheds are smaller in area, while river basins cover larger areas

options.C: River basins are smaller units formed within larger watersheds and drain limited areas
options.D: Watersheds are regions drained by groundwater, while river basins are drained by surface rivers

questions.explanation:
A river basin and a watershed differ mainly in their scale and extent.

A river basin is a large drainage area drained by a major river and its tributaries. • It represents a macro-level drainage unit. • Example: Ganga Basin, Godavari Basin, Brahmaputra Basin.

A watershed is a smaller drainage unit, usually drained by small streams, rivulets, or minor tributaries. • It represents a micro-level drainage unit. • Many small watersheds combine to form a large river basin. Additional Facts:

Hierarchical Relationship Between Basin and Watershed • Watershed → Sub-basin → River Basin 3 Hundreds or thousands of watersheds collectively form one major river basin. • This hierarchical structure is widely used in:

Water resource planning

Soil conservation

Flood control programs Concept of Water Divide:

A water divide is an elevated landform, such as: • Mountain • Ridge • Plateau edge

It separates two drainage basins.

Rainwater falling on opposite sides flows into different river systems.

Indian Examples:

Ambala Ridge • Separates the Indus Basin from the Ganga Basin.

Western Ghats • Separate the west-flowing rivers (Arabian Sea) from the east-flowing rivers (Bay of Bengal). Related Terminologies:

Catchment Area • Total area from which a river collects water. • Often used interchangeably with drainage area in practical geography.

Inland Drainage (Endorheic Basin) • Rivers do not reach the sea. • Example: Luni River draining into the Rann of Kutch.

questions.q: Which of the following forest is considered as a part of Social Forestry? 1. Urban forestry 2. Rural forestry 3. Farm forestry 4. Community forestry Select the correct answer using the codes below:

questions.explanation: Social forestry means the management and protection of forests and afforestation on barren lands with the purpose of helping in the environmental, social and rural development. The National Commission on Agriculture (1976) has classified social forestry into three categories. • Urban forestry: pertains to the raising and management of trees on public and privately owned lands in and around urban centres such as green belts, parks, roadside avenues, industrial and commercial green belts, etc. • Rural forestry: Emphasis on promotion of agro-forestry and community-forestry. • Farm forestry:. Since Community Forestry is a sub-component of Rural Forestry, it is by extension, a part of Social Forestry.

Seasonal Leaf Shedding: Trees shed their leaves during the dry summer season to reduce water loss through transpiration.

Dominant Species: The presence of teak, sal, and bamboo is a classic indicator of Tropical Deciduous Forests.

Distribution: They are the most widespread forests in India, covering large parts of the country.

questions.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Dharwar System comprises the first metamorphosed sedimentary rocks in India. 2. The Cuddapah Basin is a crescent-shaped Proterozoic basin situated in the east-central part of the Dharwar craton. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct:

The Dharwar System represents the first metamorphosed sedimentary rock system in India.

These rocks were formed after the erosion of older Archaean rocks, whose sediments were later subjected to heat and pressure, resulting in metamorphism.

Hence, Dharwar rocks are considered the earliest metamorphosed sedimentary rocks of India. Statement 2 is correct:

The Cuddapah Basin belongs to the Proterozoic era and forms part of the Purana rock system.

It is geographically known for its distinct crescent-shaped structure.

The basin is located mainly in Andhra Pradesh and lies over the eastern and central parts of the Dharwar craton. Additional Facts: Chronological Sequence of Major Rock Systems in India (Oldest to Youngest):

Archaean System • Oldest rocks in India. • Form the basement complex of the Peninsular Plateau.

Dharwar System • First metamorphosed sedimentary rocks. • Rich in metallic minerals.

Cuddapah System • Part of the Purana rock group. • Mainly composed of sedimentary rocks.

Vindhyan System • Also part of the Purana group. • Known for sandstones and limestones.

Gondwana System • Famous for coal deposits.

Tertiary System • Associated with the formation of the Himalayas.

Quaternary System • Includes alluvial deposits of the Northern Plains. Economic Importance of Dharwar Rocks

The Dharwar system is highly significant because it contains major metallic mineral deposits such as: • Iron ore • Manganese • Copper • Gold (notably in the Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka) Key Characteristics of the Cuddapah Basin

Located mainly in Andhra Pradesh.

Known for its crescent-shaped structure.

Contains limestone, slate, and asbestos, supporting cement industries in the region.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding India’s geopolitical location in the Indian Ocean: 1. India’s Exclusive Economic Zone covers an estimated area of over 2 million square kilometres. 2. The Great Channel separates India’s Indira Point from Indonesia’s Sumatra Island. 3. India’s territorial waters extend up to 24 nautical miles from the coastal baseline. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct:

India has a very large Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) extending up to 200 nautical miles from the baseline.

The total area of India’s EEZ is about 2.02 million square kilometres, which is indeed over 2 million sq km.

This zone provides India exclusive rights to marine resources, including fisheries, offshore oil, and minerals. Statement 2 is correct:

The Great Channel separates Great Nicobar Island (India) from Sumatra Island (Indonesia).

Indira Point, the southernmost point of India, lies on Great Nicobar Island near this channel.

This channel is strategically important because it lies close to major international sea routes near the Strait of Malacca. Statement 3 is incorrect:

India’s territorial waters extend only up to 12 nautical miles, not 24 nautical miles. The 24 nautical mile limit refers to the Contiguous Zone, where India has limited enforcement rights but not full sovereignty. Additional Facts:

Maritime Zones Defined Under UNCLOS

Territorial Sea — Up to 12 Nautical Miles • Full sovereignty of the coastal state. • Includes water, airspace, and seabed. • Contiguous Zone — 12 to 24 Nautical Miles

Limited rights for the enforcement of: • Customs laws • Immigration laws • Taxation laws • Pollution control

Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) — Up to 200 Nautical Miles • Exclusive rights over:

Fishing

Offshore oil and gas

Mineral extraction

Other countries retain navigation freedom. Strategic Importance of the Great Channel

Located near the western approach to the Strait of Malacca, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

Provides India a strategic advantage in monitoring maritime traffic between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific Ocean.

questions.q: Match List-I with List-II List-I (Disputed Zones) List-II (Geographical Characteristics / Treaties) a. Sir Creek 1. A strategic plateau located near the Chumbi Valley trijunction, overlooking the Siliguri Corridor. b. Kalapani 2. A 96-km tidal estuary in the Rann of Kachchh, disputed over the application of the Thalweg principle. c. Doklam 3. A high-altitude endorheic lake divided by the LAC, characterised by mountainous spurs known as ‘Fingers’. d. Pangong Tso 4. A territory in Pithoragarh, disputed over the interpretation of the Kali River’s source under the 1816 Treaty of Sagauli. Select the correct answer using the codes given below: a b c d
questions.question_type: Match the Following — Two-List Matching — Answer-Code Matrix
questions.explanation:
Sir Creek is a 96-km tidal estuary separating Gujarat (India) from Sindh (Pakistan). The dispute centres on the boundary line; India asserts the mid-channel boundary based on the internationally recognised Thalweg principle, while Pakistan claims the entire creek.

Kalapani is located in the Pithoragarh district of Uttarakhand. The dispute between India and Nepal originates from differing interpretations of the source of the Kali River, which was designated as the western boundary of Nepal by the British in the 1816 Treaty of Sagauli.

Doklam is a high-altitude plateau at the trijunction of India (Sikkim), Bhutan, and China (Chumbi Valley). Its strategic importance lies in its elevation, which provides a vantage point over India’s vulnerable Siliguri Corridor (Chicken’s Neck).

Pangong Tso is a 135-km-long endorheic lake in eastern Ladakh. The Line of Actual Control (LAC) passes through the lake. The northern bank is marked by eight mountainous spurs jutting into the lake, geographically referred to as “Fingers,” which form the basis of the territorial claims between India and China.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Pamir Knot: 1. The Karakoram Range extends southeastward from the Pamir Knot into the Indian subcontinent. 2. The Hindu Kush mountain range radiates eastward from the Pamir Knot towards Tibet. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct:

The Karakoram Range extends southeastward from the Pamir Knot.

This range enters the region of Ladakh and forms part of the Trans-Himalayan system.

It includes some of the highest peaks in the world, such as K2, and acts as an important high mountain barrier in northern India. Statement 2 is incorrect:

The Hindu Kush Range does not extend eastward from the Pamir Knot.

Instead, it extends westward and southwestward, forming the mountainous backbone of Afghanistan and parts of Pakistan.

The range extending eastward from the Pamir Knot toward Tibet is the Kunlun Range, not the Hindu Kush. Additional Facts:

The Pamir Knot as a Mountain Hub • The Pamir Knot is a major mountain junction in Central Asia. • Several important mountain ranges radiate outward from this region in different directions. Major Mountain Ranges Radiating from the Pamir Knot

Southeastward • Karakoram Range

Followed further south by the Himalayas

West and Southwest • Hindu Kush Range

Extends across Afghanistan and Pakistan.

East 3 Kunlun Mountains

Forms the northern boundary of the Tibetan Plateau.

Northeast • Tian Shan Mountains

It extends into Central Asia and western China. Trans-Himalayan Ranges:

The following ranges belong to the TransHimalayan system: • Karakoram Range • Ladakh Range • Zaskar Range

These ranges lie north of the main Himalayan ranges and are geologically older than the Himalayas. Key Geographic Importance:

The Pamir Knot is often referred to as the “Roof of the World” due to its very high elevation.

It plays a critical role in the formation and distribution of major Asian mountain systems.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Brahmaputra River: 1. It originates from the Chemayungdung glacier near Mansarovar Lake. 2. In Bangladesh, the Teesta joins it on the left bank, after which it is called the Jamuna. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers of the world, has its origin in the Chemayungdung glacier of the Kailash range near the Mansarovar lake. From here, it traverses eastward longitudinally for a distance of nearly 1,200 km in a dry and flat region of southern Tibet, where it is known as the Tsangpo, which means ‘the purifier.’

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Brahmaputra enters into Bangladesh near Dhubri and flows southward. In Bangladesh, the Teesta joins it on its right bank from where the river is known as the Jamuna. It finally merges with the river Padma, which falls in the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: The British selected Darjeeling as a hill station and tea-growing centre due to certain favourable physiographic conditions. Which of the following characteristics of the Darjeeling Himalayas best explains this choice?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: The dominance of extensive Karewa terrace deposits.
options.B: The conspicuous absence of the Shiwalik formations.

Because of this, the mountains descend abruptly into the plains, forming Duar (Door) formations.

The Duars of the Darjeeling–Sikkim Himalayas • The Duars are foothill plains formed where mountains descend into the plains. • The term “Duar” means “door”, as these areas serve as gateways between the plains and the hills. • The Teesta River system dominates this region and contributes to deep valley formation. questions.q: Which of the following characteristics are typical of the minor west-flowing rivers originating from the Western Ghats? 1. They are generally steep and fast-flowing. 2. They form extensive deltas along the western coast. 3. They discharge directly into the Arabian Sea. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is Correct:

Minor west-flowing rivers from the Western Ghats are steep and fast-flowing.

They originate at high elevations in the Western Ghats and travel a short distance to the Arabian Sea.

This creates a steep gradient, resulting in rapid flow and high erosive power. Statement 2 is Incorrect:

These rivers do not form extensive deltas.

Because they are short and swift, they carry limited sediment and lack broad coastal plains needed for delta formation.

Instead, they typically form estuaries along the western coast. Statement 3 is Correct:

These rivers flow westward directly into the Arabian Sea.

The Western Ghats act as a major water divide, directing rainfall on the western slopes toward the Arabian Sea. Additional Facts:

Key Characteristics of Minor West-Flowing Rivers • Short length, generally less than 100 km. • Steep gradient due to elevated origin. • Fast-flowing nature with strong erosional activity. • Formation of estuaries, not deltas. • High potential for hydroelectric power generation. Important Examples of West-Flowing Rivers:

Goa • Mandovi River • Zuari River

Presence of estuaries rather than deltas.

Role of the Western Ghats as a Water Divide

Rain falling on the western slopes flows into the Arabian Sea.

Rain falling on the eastern slopes feeds long rivers like: • Godavari • Krishna • Kaveri

questions.q: The Kayals of Kerala are best described as which of the following?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Kayals of Kerala are best described as lagoons.

In Kerala, the term Kayal refers to backwaters, which are long, narrow water bodies running parallel to the coast.

These water bodies are separated from the Arabian Sea by sand bars or barrier islands, which is the defining feature of lagoons.

The water in Kayals is typically brackish, as it contains both seawater and freshwater from rivers.

Their structure and coastal formation clearly match the geographical definition of lagoons. Additional Facts:

Major Kayals of Kerala • Vembanad Kayal

Often called the “Rice Bowl of Kerala.”

questions.q: Which of the following saline lakes in India is uniquely renowned for yielding high-quality salt with a sodium chloride content of nearly 98%?

questions.explanation:
Pachpadra Lake is uniquely known for producing high-quality salt with nearly 98% Sodium Chloride (NaCl) content.

Pachpadra Lake, located in the Barmer district of Rajasthan, produces salt of exceptionally high chemical purity.

The salt obtained here contains about 98% Sodium Chloride, making it suitable for direct consumption with minimal refining.

Because of this purity, Pachpadra Lake is widely recognized as the most important source of high-quality edible salt among the saline lakes of Rajasthan. Additional Facts:

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the regional sub-divisions of the Gangetic Plain: 1. The Rohilkhand plain forms the northwestern part of the Upper Ganga plain, directly bordering the Aravalli range. 2. The Awadh plain is located in the Middle Ganga plain, primarily drained by the Ghaghara river. 3. The Rarh region is a lateritic soil transition zone situated west of the Bhagirathi-Hooghly river. Statement 1 is incorrect:

The Rohilkhand Plain forms part of the Upper Ganga Plain in northern Uttar Pradesh (including Bareilly and Moradabad).

However, it does not border the Aravalli Range.

Its northern boundary is formed by the Himalayan foothills (Shiwaliks/Kumaon region), while the Aravalli Range lies far to the southwest. Statement 2 is correct:

The Awadh Plain lies in the Middle Ganga Plain, mainly in central Uttar Pradesh.

It is drained primarily by the Ghaghara River, along with tributaries such as the Gomti. Statement 3 is correct:

The Rarh region is located west of the Bhagirathi–Hooghly River in West Bengal.

It is characterized by lateritic soils, representing a transition zone between the Chotanagpur Plateau and the alluvial plains of Bengal.

Therefore, this statement is correct. Additional Facts:

Sub-divisions of the Gangetic Plain

The Gangetic Plain is divided into three major regional sections:

Includes: • Ganga–Yamuna Doab • Rohilkhand Plain

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the badland topography of the Malwa Plateau: 1. The extensive badland topography of this region is primarily caused by deep gully erosion. 2. The Chambal river, originating from the Amarkantak plateau, is the primary agent forming these ravines. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is Correct:

The badland topography of the Malwa Plateau is mainly formed due to deep gully erosion.

During heavy monsoon rains, surface runoff cuts into the soft soil, forming rills, which later deepen into gullies.

Over time, these gullies expand into ravines, creating rugged and highly dissected terrain known as badlands or “bihads”.

This type of erosion is especially prominent along the Chambal River basin. Statement 2 is Incorrect:

The Chambal River does not originate from the Amarkantak Plateau.

It originates near Janapav (close to Mhow) in the Vindhya Range of Madhya Pradesh.

The Amarkantak Plateau is actually the source of rivers such as: • Narmada (flows west) • Son (flows northeast) • Tributaries of the Mahanadi Additional Facts: Formation of Badland Topography Badlands develop through a progressive erosion process:

Sheet Erosion • Thin layer of topsoil removed uniformly.

Rill Erosion • Small channels form due to flowing water.

Gully Erosion • Channels deepen into permanent gullies. • Leads to formation of ravines, the main feature of badlands.

Chambal Ravines Region: • Found mainly along the Chambal River basin. • Spread across:

Madhya Pradesh (Morena, Bhind)

Rajasthan (Dholpur)

Uttar Pradesh (Etawah)

These ravines form one of India’s most extensive badland landscapes. The Amarkantak Plateau as a Radial Drainage Centre: The Amarkantak Plateau is known for radial drainage, where rivers flow in different directions:

West: Narmada River

North-East: Son River

South: Tributaries of the Mahanadi

North: Johila River Why Badlands Are Problematic:

Soil becomes unsuitable for agriculture.

Land is fragmented into deep trenches and gullies.

Requires reclamation measures such as: • Afforestation • Check dams • Soil conservation methods

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding tropical cyclones in India: 1. Heavy river discharge into the Bay of Bengal creates layered waters, limiting mixing with cooler deep water. 2. Strong vertical wind differences over the Arabian Sea help the strengthening of tropical cyclones. 3. Weak low-pressure systems from the South China Sea often enter the Bay of Bengal, supporting cyclone formation. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Heavy river discharge into the Bay of Bengal creates layered waters, limiting mixing with cooler deep water.

The Bay of Bengal receives massive freshwater discharge from rivers such as: • Ganga • Brahmaputra • Mahanadi • Godavari

This creates: • A low-salinity surface layer • Stratified (layered) water structure

Effect: • Prevents vertical mixing with cooler deep water • Keeps sea surface temperature high (above 26.5°C) • Warm surface water supports cyclone formation and intensification Statement 2 is incorrect: Strong vertical wind differences over the Arabian Sea help the strengthening of tropical cyclones.

Vertical wind shear refers to changes in wind speed and direction with height.

Strong vertical wind shear: • Disrupts cyclone structure • Tilts the vertical column of rising air • Prevents cyclone intensification

Arabian Sea condition: • Historically has higher vertical wind shear • This reduces cyclone formation, not increases it Statement 3 is correct: Weak low-pressure systems from the South China Sea often enter the Bay of Bengal, supporting cyclone formation.

Many cyclones in the Bay of Bengal: • Begin as remnants of typhoons from the South China Sea

Process: • These systems cross Southeast Asia • Enter the Bay of Bengal • Re-intensify over warm ocean waters

This contributes significantly to: • Higher cyclone frequency in the Bay of Bengal

Loses contact with the rock face during the fall

Drops freely due to formation of an overhang. Formation mechanism: • River flows over:

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Telangana and Rayalaseema plateaus: 1. The Rayalaseema plateau features the crescent-shaped Cuddapah basin, rich in limestone and quartzite formations. 2. The Telangana plateau predominantly consists of Archaean gneisses and relies heavily on tank irrigation. 3. Rayalaseema receives significantly higher southwest monsoon rainfall compared to the Telangana plateau region. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct:

The Rayalaseema Plateau contains the Cuddapah Basin, a well-known Proterozoic sedimentary basin.

The basin is crescent-shaped, which is a commonly tested geomorphological feature.

It is rich in important sedimentary rocks such as: • Limestone — widely used in the cement industries • Quartzite — used in construction and industrial applications

The abundance of limestone has led to the development of major cement industries in the Rayalaseema region. Statement 2 is correct:

The Telangana Plateau is composed mainly of ancient Archaean gneisses, typical of the Indian Shield region.

Due to the hard, rocky terrain and undulating surface, groundwater storage is limited.

As a result, the region traditionally relies on tank irrigation, where rainwater is stored in small reservoirs or tanks.

This irrigation method has historical importance and has been revived through initiatives such as Mission Kakatiya. Statement 3 is incorrect:

The statement incorrectly claims that Rayalaseema receives significantly higher Southwest Monsoon rainfall than Telangana.

In reality, Rayalaseema is one of the driest regions of India, located in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.

Telangana receives relatively more Southwest Monsoon rainfall than Rayalaseema. Additional Facts:

Rayalaseema Plateau — Key Features • Location:

Southern part of Andhra Pradesh • Important geological feature:

Cuddapah Basin — crescent-shaped sedimentary basin • Major minerals:

Limestone

Barytes

Quartzite • Drainage system:

This region is drained by the Krishna, Tungabhadra, and Pennar river systems. • Climate feature:

Lies in the rain shadow zone of the Western Ghats, resulting in low rainfall. Telangana Plateau — Key Features:

Rock structure: • Dominated by Archaean gneissic rocks

Drainage system: • Drained mainly by the Godavari and Krishna river systems.

Irrigation pattern: • Heavy reliance on tank irrigation due to limited groundwater storage.

Major mineral region: • Singareni coalfields are an important source of coal. Rainfall Contrast Between the Two Regions

Telangana Plateau: • Receives moderate rainfall from the Southwest Monsoon.

Rayalaseema Plateau: • Receives comparatively low Southwest Monsoon rainfall. • Sometimes receives additional rainfall from the Northeast Monsoon, but overall remains drought-prone.

questions.q: Which of the following statements most accurately describes the ‘Bhur’ formations found in the Upper Ganga plain?

options.A: Elevated, wind-blown sandy tracts in the Bhangar region that are generally less fertile for agriculture.

questions.explanation:
Bhur formations are elevated, sandy tracts found mainly in the Upper Ganga Plain, especially in western Uttar Pradesh.

They are formed by aeolian (wind-blown) deposition of sand, particularly during dry summer months when strong winds carry loose sand from riverbeds.

These sandy deposits usually occur over the Bhangar (old alluvial) terraces.

Because the soil is sandy and highly porous, it does not retain moisture well and is therefore less fertile for agriculture compared to the surrounding alluvial plains. Additional Facts:

Bhur — Key Characteristics

Location: • Found mainly in the Upper Ganga Plain, especially in districts such as:

Bijnor

Moradabad

Rampur

Formation process: • Created by wind deposition of sand (aeolian action).

Soil nature: • Sandy • Highly porous • Low water retention capacity

Agricultural value: • Generally less fertile than the surrounding alluvial soils.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the mudbanks or the Chakara phenomenon: 1. It involves the suspension of fine clay that naturally slow down wave action to create calm waters. 2. It is a unique oceanographic feature occurring exclusively along the Coromandel coast during the northeast monsoon. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct:

The Chakara (mudbank) phenomenon involves the suspension of fine clay and mud particles in coastal waters.

This suspended mud absorbs wave energy, reducing turbulence and creating unusually calm water patches even during rough sea conditions.

This calm zone forms naturally during the Southwest Monsoon and supports intensive fishing activity. Statement 2 is incorrect:

The statement wrongly places the Chakara phenomenon on the Coromandel Coast during the Northeast Monsoon.

In reality, the Chakara phenomenon occurs: • Along the Malabar Coast (Kerala) • During the Southwest Monsoon (June to September)

It is particularly observed near Alappuzha and Kollam along Kerala’s coast. Additional Facts:

Chakara (Mudbanks): • Location:

Found along the Malabar Coast of Kerala, especially near Alappuzha and Kollam. • Season of occurrence:

Occurs during the Southwest Monsoon. • Main feature:

Formation of calm water patches amidst rough monsoon seas. • Economic importance:

Supports intensive fishing, especially for prawns and fish, during monsoon months. Possible Causes of Chakara Formation:

Wave-mud interaction theory: • The Southwest Monsoon swells churn up and suspend bottom sediments, creating a viscous fluid mud layer that then dissipates wave energy.

Subterranean water theory: • Underground water pressure forces fine mud upward through the seabed.

Backwater discharge theory: • Sediments from Kerala’s backwaters (Kayals) enter the sea during heavy monsoon discharge. Malabar vs Coromandel Coast: Key Differences

Malabar Coast: • Faces the Arabian Sea • Receives heavy Southwest Monsoon rainfall • Known for backwaters (Kayals) • Experiences the Chakara phenomenon

Coromandel Coast: • Faces the Bay of Bengal • Receives major rainfall from the Northeast Monsoon • Does not experience Chakara mudbanks

The Gulf of Kutch has one of the highest tidal range in India, reaching up to about 8 metres.

Its funnel-shaped coastline enhances tidal movement, making it the most suitable location in India for tidal power projects. Major west-flowing rivers like the Narmada and Tapi drain directly into the Gulf of Khambhat.

The Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) receives waters from major west-flowing rivers such as: • Narmada • Tapi • Mahi • Sabarmati

These rivers form large estuaries rather than deltas due to steep gradients. The Gulf of Mannar is geographically characterised by a rich marine biosphere reserve and coral reefs.

The Gulf of Mannar is known for its rich biodiversity, including: • Coral reefs • Seagrass beds

Highest tidal range in India • Economic importance:

Suitable for tidal energy development

Houses Marine National Park (Jamnagar). Gulf of Khambhat — Key Features

This statement is incorrect because peninsular rivers are generally seasonal (non-perennial).

They lack glacial sources and depend almost entirely on monsoon rainfall.

During the dry summer months, their discharge reduces sharply, and many smaller rivers may dry up, leaving isolated pools in rocky channels.

Groundwater base flow alone is not sufficient to sustain perennial flow in most peninsular rivers. Additional Facts:

questions.q: Based on geological structure and formation, which of the following mountain ranges is NOT an example of a block mountain?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Aravalli Range: • The Aravalli Range is one of the oldest fold mountains in the world, formed during the Precambrian era. • It originated due to compressional tectonic forces, where crustal plates converged and folded the rocks. • Over millions of years, it has undergone intense erosion, reducing its height significantly. • Because of this long erosion history, it is now classified as a relict (residual) fold mountain, not a block mountain.

Satpura Range: • The Satpura Range is a classic block mountain (horst). • It was formed due to faulting, where land blocks were uplifted along fractures in the Earth’s crust. • It lies south of the Narmada Rift Valley, which represents a graben (down-faulted block).

Vindhyan Range: • The Vindhyan Range is also associated with fault-block formation. • It forms the northern boundary of the Narmada Rift Valley. • Like the Satpuras, it represents an uplifted block (horst) created by crustal faulting.

Nilgiri Hills: • The Nilgiri Hills are considered fault-block mountains. • They were uplifted due to tectonic faulting along the margins of the Deccan Plateau. • They form the junction of the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats.

Key Concept Summary: • Fold Mountains formation mechanism: • Formed by the compression of tectonic plates.

Examples: • Himalayas (young fold mountains) • Aravalli Range (old fold mountains)

Important point: • Old fold mountains like the Aravallis are now heavily eroded and classified as relic mountains. Block Mountains

Formation mechanism: • Formed by faulting, where large crustal blocks are uplifted or dropped.

Key associated terms: • Horst → Raised block (mountain) • Graben → Dropped block (rift valley)

Examples in India: • Satpura Range • Vindhyan Range • Nilgiri Hills

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD): 1. A Positive IOD shows unusually warm waters in the eastern Indian Ocean, strengthening the Indian summer monsoon. 2. A Negative IOD leads to a deeper thermocline in the western Indian Ocean, increasing moisture supply to the monsoon. 3. Rising air activity over the western Indian Ocean during a Positive IOD can reduce drought effects caused by El Niño. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is incorrect:

In a Positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD): • Western Indian Ocean (near East Africa) becomes warmer than normal. • Eastern Indian Ocean (near Indonesia/ Australia) becomes cooler than normal. Statement 2 is incorrect:

During a Negative IOD: • Western Indian Ocean becomes cooler than normal. • The thermocline becomes shallower, not deeper, in the western region. • This reduces convection and weakens moisture supply, often leading to deficient monsoon rainfall in India. Statement 3 is correct:

During a Positive IOD: • Warm waters in the western Indian Ocean cause strong convection and rising air. • This enhances moisture transport toward India. • If a Positive IOD coincides with El Niño, it can partially offset El Niño’s weakening effect on the monsoon, reducing drought risk. Key Concept Summary:

Positive Indian Ocean Dipole (Positive IOD) • Sea surface temperature pattern:

Western Indian Ocean → Warmer

Eastern Indian Ocean → Cooler • Atmospheric effect:

Strong convection over the western Indian Ocean

Enhanced monsoon rainfall over India

Can neutralise El Niño drought effects • Thermocline pattern:

Deeper in the west

Shallower in the east

Negative Indian Ocean Dipole (Negative IOD) • Sea surface temperature pattern:

Western Indian Ocean → Cooler

Eastern Indian Ocean → Warmer • Atmospheric effect:

Moisture shifts toward Indonesia and Australia

Weak Indian monsoon

Increased drought risk in India • Thermocline pattern:

Shallower in the west

Deeper in the east

questions.q: Consider the following pairs of Mega Multipurpose River Valley Projects and their specific geographical or state-sharing characteristics: 1. Bhakra Nangal Project : Forms the Gobind Sagar reservoir on the Sutlej river. 2. Tehri Dam Project : Located precisely at the confluence of the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers. 3. Sardar Sarovar Project : Rajasthan receives a share of the irrigation water but no share of the generated hydroelectric power. 4. Hirakud Project : Primarily constructed across the Mahanadi river to mitigate flooding in the coastal delta region of Odisha. How many pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correct: Bhakra Nangal Project — Forms the Gobind Sagar reservoir on the Sutlej River. • The Bhakra Nangal Dam is constructed across the Sutlej River. • The reservoir created behind the dam is called Gobind Sagar. • It is one of India’s major multipurpose river valley projects, providing irrigation, hydropower, and flood control.

Pair 2 is incorrect: Tehri Dam Project — Located precisely at the confluence of the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers. • This pair is incorrect. • The confluence of the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers is called Devprayag, where the river officially takes the name Ganga. • The Tehri Dam is not located there. • It is built on the Bhagirathi River at its confluence with the Bhilangna River, upstream of Devprayag.

Pair 3 is correct: Sardar Sarovar Project — Rajasthan receives a share of the irrigation water but no share of the generated hydroelectric power. • This pair is correct. • The Sardar Sarovar Project is built on the Narmada River. • Rajasthan receives irrigation water through the Narmada Canal. 3 However, Rajasthan does not receive any share of the hydroelectric power generated by the project.

Pair 4 is correct: Hirakud Project — Primarily constructed across the Mahanadi river to mitigate flooding in the coastal delta region of Odisha. • This pair is correct. • The Hirakud Dam is constructed across the Mahanadi River in Odisha. • One of its primary purposes was flood control, as the Mahanadi frequently caused destructive floods in the delta region before the dam was built.

questions.q: The Saltoro Ridge, associated with the Siachen Glacier region, is a sub-range of which of the following mountain ranges?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Saltoro Ridge: • The Saltoro Ridge is a sub-range of the Karakoram Range. • It lies west of the Siachen Glacier and forms its southwestern boundary. • The ridge separates the Siachen Glacier basin from the valleys lying to the west. • Because it is structurally part of the Karakoram system, the correct answer is Karakoram Range.

Ladakh Range: • The Ladakh Range lies south of the Karakoram Range. • It is separated from the Karakoram by the Shyok River valley. • Since Saltoro Ridge lies within the Karakoram system, it cannot belong to the Ladakh Range.

Zaskar Range: • The Zaskar Range lies further south, beyond the Indus River. • Therefore, it is geographically distinct from the Saltoro Ridge.

Pir Panjal Range:

The Pir Panjal Range is also part of the Lesser Himalayas.

It lies even further south and encloses the Kashmir Valley.

It is completely separate from the Karakoram mountain system. Key Geographical Framework: North-to-South Sequence of Major Ranges in This Region

Karakoram Range • Northernmost • Includes Saltoro Ridge • Contains major glaciers such as the Siachen Glacier

Ladakh Range • Lies between the Shyok River and the Indus River

Zaskar Range • Located south of the Indus River

Pir Panjal Range • Part of the Lesser Himalayas • Surrounds the Kashmir Valley Additional High-Value Facts: Strategic Importance of Saltoro Ridge

Controls access to the Siachen Glacier region.

Major passes located here include: • Sia La • Bilafond La

The ridge plays a critical role in defining military positions in the region.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Ghaggar–Hakra river system is correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: It is a year-round Himalayan river that acts as a major left-bank tributary of the Indus.
options.B: The river rises in the Dagshai hills of the Shiwaliks and ends as an inland-draining river in the Thar Desert.
options.C: It flows across the Malwa Plateau and is the main cause of gully erosion in Rajasthan.
options.D: The river system flows entirely within the boundaries of India.

questions.explanation:
Statement B is correct: The river rises in the Dagshai hills of the Shiwaliks and ends as an inland-draining river in the Thar Desert.

The Ghaggar River originates in the Dagshai Hills of the Shiwalik Range in Himachal Pradesh.

It flows through Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan.

In Rajasthan, the river loses its flow and disappears into the sands of the Thar Desert, making it an inland-draining (endorheic) river system.

Its downstream continuation in Pakistan is known as the Hakra River. Statement A is incorrect: It is a year-round Himalayan river that acts as a major left-bank tributary of the Indus.

The Ghaggar is not a perennial Himalayan river.

It is a seasonal (ephemeral) river, flowing mainly during the monsoon.

It does not join the Indus River; instead, it disappears in the desert. Statement C is incorrect: It flows across the Malwa Plateau and is the main cause of gully erosion in Rajasthan. The river associated with gully erosion (ravines) in the Malwa Plateau is the Chambal River, not the Ghaggar.

The Chambal basin is famous for its deep ravines, especially in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. Statement D is incorrect: The river system flows entirely within the boundaries of India.

While the Ghaggar flows in India, its continuation, called the Hakra River, extends into Pakistan, where it dissipates in the Cholistan Desert.

Therefore, the system crosses international boundaries. Summary:

Ghaggar–Hakra River System — Essential Facts • Origin:

Dagshai Hills, Shiwalik Range, Himachal Pradesh • Nature:

Seasonal (ephemeral) river • Drainage type:

Inland drainage (endorheic system)

Disappears in the Thar Desert • Course through India:

Himachal Pradesh

Punjab

Haryana

Rajasthan • Continuation outside India:

Known as the Hakra River in Pakistan

Disappears in the Cholistan Desert Additional High-Value Facts:

Historical Importance • Many Indus Valley Civilisation (Harappan) sites developed along the Ghaggar basin. • Important archaeological sites include:

Kalibangan (Rajasthan)

Banawali (Haryana)

questions.q: Which of the following pairs of strategic offshore islands and their geographical importance is incorrect?

options.A: Wheeler Island (Kalam Island) : Located off the coast of Odisha and used as India’s main missile testing centre.
options.B: Sagar Island : It is used as an important monitoring point for cyclones coming from the Arabian Sea.
options.C: Pamban Island : Located between India and Sri Lanka and marks the starting point of Rama Setu (Adam’s Bridge) near Dhanushkodi.
options.D: Sriharikota Island : A barrier island in Andhra Pradesh that separates Pulicat Lake from the Bay of Bengal.

questions.explanation:
Pair A is correct: Wheeler Island (Kalam Island) — Located off the coast of Odisha and used as India’s main missile testing centre. • Wheeler Island, officially called Dr. Abdul Kalam Island, lies off the Odisha coast. • It houses the Integrated Test Range (ITR), India’s principal facility for testing ballistic missiles such as Agni and Prithvi.

Pair B is incorrect: Sagar Island — It is used as an important monitoring point for cyclones coming from the Arabian Sea. • Sagar Island is located in the Ganga delta in West Bengal, at the mouth of the Hooghly River. • It lies in the Bay of Bengal, not near the Arabian Sea. • Therefore, it cannot monitor cyclones from the Arabian Sea, which lies on the western side of India.

Pair C is correct: Pamban Island — Located between India and Sri Lanka and marks the starting point of Rama Setu near Dhanushkodi. • Pamban Island (also known as Rameswaram Island) lies between India and Sri Lanka. • The town of Dhanushkodi, located at its eastern tip, marks the starting point of the chain of limestone shoals known as Rama Setu (Adam’s Bridge).

Pair D is correct: Sriharikota Island — A barrier island in Andhra Pradesh that separates Pulicat Lake from the Bay of Bengal. • Sriharikota is a classic barrier island along the Andhra Pradesh coast. • It separates Pulicat Lake from the Bay of Bengal. • The island hosts the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, India’s primary satellite launch site.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the geomorphological reasons behind the shifting courses of rivers like the Kosi? 1. The Kosi River is characterized by an exceptionally high sediment load derived from the fragile and tectonically active Himalayas. 2. The sudden decrease in channel gradient as the river enters the plains of Bihar leads to rapid aggradation (deposition) of the riverbed. 3. The consistent westward migration of the Kosi is primarily attributed to the tectonic tilting of the Indo-Gangetic Foredeep towards the west. 4. “Avulsion” in the Kosi river occurs when the riverbed becomes higher than the surrounding floodplains due to continuous siltation. Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Kosi River is characterised by an exceptionally high sediment load derived from the fragile and tectonically active Himalayas. • The Kosi River originates in the young Himalayan mountains, which are geologically unstable and prone to erosion. • Due to steep slopes and fragile rocks, the river carries huge quantities of sediment, including silt, sand, and pebbles. • This heavy sediment load is one of the main reasons for its unstable and shifting course.

Statement 2 is correct: The sudden decrease in channel gradient as the river enters the plains of Bihar leads to rapid aggradation (deposition) of the riverbed. 3 When the Kosi flows from the steep Himalayan region into the flat plains of North Bihar, its velocity reduces sharply. • The river loses the energy required to transport sediment. • As a result, rapid deposition (aggradation) occurs, raising the riverbed and increasing flood risk.

Statement 3 is incorrect: The consistent westward migration of the Kosi is primarily attributed to the tectonic tilting of the IndoGangetic Foredeep towards the west. • This statement is incorrect because the westward shifting of the Kosi is mainly due to sediment-driven processes, not tectonic tilting. • The river frequently changes course because it deposits sediment and blocks its own path, forcing it to seek a new, lower route. • This repeated shifting occurs across its large alluvial fan, not because of consistent tectonic movement.

Statement 4 is correct: “Avulsion” in the Kosi river occurs when the riverbed becomes higher than the surrounding floodplains due to continuous siltation. • This statement correctly defines avulsion. • Continuous deposition raises the riverbed above the surrounding land, making it unstable. • During heavy floods, the river breaks embankments and suddenly shifts to a new channel at a lower level. • The Kosi River is a classic example of an avulsing river.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding ‘Usar’ lands found in the Ganga Plains: 1. Usar lands are formed due to the upward movement of saline and alkaline salts to the surface, caused by poor drainage and a high water table. 2. The application of gypsum is a common method to reclaim Usar lands, as it helps reduce soil alkalinity and restore soil fertility. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Usar lands are formed due to the upward movement of saline and alkaline salts to the surface, caused by poor drainage and a high water table.

3 ‘Usar’ is the traditional term used for saltaffected soils (both saline and alkaline), especially in the Ganga Plains such as western Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana. • These soils commonly develop in areas with extensive canal irrigation, where excess water leads to waterlogging and a rise in the groundwater table. • During hot seasons, capillary action pulls dissolved salts (such as sodium, magnesium, and calcium salts) upward from the groundwater to the soil surface. • When the water evaporates, it leaves behind a white salt crust, making the soil toxic and unsuitable for crops.

Statement 2 is correct: The application of gypsum is a common method to reclaim Usar lands, as it helps reduce soil alkalinity and restore soil fertility. • Gypsum (calcium sulfate) is the most widely used chemical amendment for reclaiming alkaline (sodic) Usar soils. • In these soils, excess sodium binds tightly to clay particles, making the soil compact and impermeable. • When gypsum is applied:

Calcium replaces sodium on clay particles.

The released sodium is then leached downward below the root zone using irrigation water.

This process restores soil structure and improves agricultural productivity. Additional facts: Salt-Affected Soils

Local Names of Salt-Affected Soils • These soils are known by different regional terms across North India: • Reh • Kallar • Usar • Thur • Chopan • Karl Key Physical Process:

The upward movement of salts occurs due to capillary action, not leaching.

Capillary action allows water to move upward against gravity through fine soil pores.

This process becomes intense when: • The water table is high • Evaporation rates are high • Drainage is poor

Important distinction: • Capillary action → brings salts upward • Leaching → washes salts downward Saline vs. Alkaline Soil Reclamation

Saline soils • Contain neutral soluble salts • Reclaimed mainly by leaching with fresh water

Alkaline (sodic) soils • Contain excess sodium • Require gypsum application first, followed by leaching Biological Reclamation Method

After gypsum treatment, farmers often grow salt-tolerant green manure crops.

The most commonly used crop is:

Dhaincha (Sesbania) • A nitrogen-fixing legume • Improves soil organic matter • Helps lower soil pH • Enhances long-term soil fertility

questions.q: Which is the northernmost island of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands group?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Landfall Island: Sits at the very top of the island chain. It is strategically significant because it is the closest Indian territory to Myanmar, separated from Myanmar’s Coco Islands by the Coco Channel.

North Andaman Island: The main northern landmass, located just south of Landfall Island (separated by the Cleugh Passage). It houses Saddle Peak, the highest point in the archipelago.

Narcondam Island: It is located in the Andaman Sea, far to the east of the main island chain, and is a dormant volcano.

Smith Island: Located slightly further south, just off the east coast of North Andaman.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Wular Lake: 1. Geologically, Wular Lake is classified as a tectonic lake, formed as a result of subsidence of the earth’s crust within a synclinal trough. 2. The Tulbul Navigation Project is located at the point where the Jhelum River enters Wular Lake to regulate water flow. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Wular Lake is classified as a tectonic lake formed due to subsidence of the earth’s crust within a synclinal trough. • Wular Lake, located in Jammu and Kashmir, is a tectonic lake. • It was formed due to subsidence (downward movement) of the earth’s crust in a synclinal trough within the Kashmir Valley. • Although the Jhelum River feeds the lake, its basin originated primarily due to tectonic activity, not river erosion.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Tulbul Navigation Project is located at the point where the Jhelum River enters Wular Lake.

Tulbul Navigation Project is located at the outlet (exit) of Wular Lake, not at the entry point.

It is situated near Sopore, where the Jhelum River flows out of Wular Lake.

The project functions as a navigation lock-cumcontrol structure, designed to regulate water release from the lake to maintain sufficient depth in the Jhelum River during winter months. Additional Facts:

Jhelum River — Key Geographical Points • Origin:

The Jhelum River originates from the Verinag Spring at the foothills of the Pir Panjal Range. • Unique feature:

Unlike most Himalayan rivers, the Jhelum forms large meanders within the Kashmir Valley because the valley floor is relatively flat. • Flow through Wular Lake:

The Jhelum enters Wular Lake from the southeast.

It exits from the western side, continuing toward Pakistan. Wular Lake:

Acts as a natural flood reservoir for the Jhelum River.

Helps regulate seasonal flooding in the Kashmir Valley.

It is one of the largest freshwater lakes in India. Lake Types:

Tectonic lakes • Formed due to crustal movements • Example: Dal Lake, Wular Lake

Glacial lakes • Formed by glacier erosion • Examples: Roopkund

Crater lakes • Formed by a meteorite impact • Example: Lonar Lake Lagoon lakes • Formed along coasts by sand barriers • Examples: Chilika Lake, Pulicat Lake

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a centripetal drainage pattern?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Streams radiate outwards from a central dome or volcanic cone in all directions.
options.B: Rivers discharge their waters from all directions into a central lake or depression.
options.C: The primary river is joined by its tributaries at roughly right angles along a folded structure.
options.D:
Multiple streams flow in the same general direction, following the steep regional slope.

SPACE FOR ROUGH WORK

SPACE FOR ROUGH WORK

questions.explanation:
Centripetal Drainage:

The term centripetal means centre-seeking.

In a centripetal drainage pattern, the surrounding land is higher, forming a basin or depression in the middle.

Rivers and streams flow inward from all directions toward this central low point.

Water usually collects in a lake, playa, or inland basin.

Indian Examples: • Loktak Lake (Manipur) — A classic basin receiving drainage from surrounding hills. • Sambhar Lake (Rajasthan) — A closed inland basin where streams flow inward. Radial drainage:

Rivers flow outward from a central high point, such as: • Volcanic cones • Domes • Plateau peaks

It is the opposite of centripetal drainage.

Indian Example: • Amarkantak Plateau, from where rivers flow in different outward directions. Trellis drainage:

Forms in regions with alternating hard and soft rock layers.

Tributaries join the main river at right angles.

Common in folded mountain regions. Parallel drainage:

Develops where there is a uniform steep slope.

Streams flow almost parallel to each other.

Indian Example: • Short west-flowing rivers from the Western Ghats into the Arabian Sea. Dendritic Drainage:

Key feature: • Resembles branches of a tree
